## [pnpm 12 Beta 0](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v12.0.0-beta.0)
*GitHub Releases · pnpm* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.70
Tags: product_launch, github_release, developer_tool, cli_tool, tool_update

> <h2>Minor Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p>The Rust engine now reads four more settings from <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> and <code>PNPM_CONFIG_*</code>, instead of only accepting them as CLI flags:</p> <ul> <li><code>frozenLockfile</code> — <code>pnpm install</code> grows a <code>--no-frozen-lockfile</code> flag so the setting can be overridden in both directions. As in pnpm, it cannot be set in the global <code>config.yaml</code>.</li> <li><code>savePrefix</code> — the range operator <code>pnpm add</code> saves, still overridable with <code>--save-prefix</code> / <code>--save-exact</code>.</li> <li><code>savePeer</code> — <code>pnpm add</code> also records the new dependency in <code>peerDependencies</code>. <code>pnpm add --no-save-peer</code> overrides it back off.</li> <li><code>saveCatalogName</code> — the catalog <code>pnpm add</code> saves into.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>The Rust engine now supports the <code>saveWorkspaceProtocol</code> setting, so <code>pnpm add <pkg>@workspace:…</code> writes back the same specifier pnpm does. Under the default <code>rolling</code>, a request like <code>workspace:^1.2.3</code> is saved as <code>workspace:^</code> — a range with no version in it, so bumping the workspace package never has to touch its dependents' manifests. <code>saveWorkspaceProtocol: true</code> saves the workspace package's resolved version instead (<code>workspace:^2.5.0</code>), and <code>false</code> keeps the <code>workspace:</code> form only when it was asked for explicitly. Previously the specifier was written back exactly as typed.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --workspace</code> is supported: dependencies that a workspace project publishes are re-pointed at the local copies through the <code>workspace:</code> protocol. The <code>saveWorkspaceProtocol</code> setting is honored — under its <code>rolling</code> default an entry becomes <code>workspace:*</code>, <code>workspace:^</code>, or <code>workspace:~</code> (whichever matches the range it already declared), so a sibling's next release does not invalidate it. Naming a dependency that is not in the workspace fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_WORKSPACE_PACKAGE_NOT_FOUND</code>, and combining the flag with <code>--latest</code> fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_BAD_OPTIONS</code>.</p> <p><code>pnpm update --depth <number></code> is now applied per dependency instead of only distinguishing <code>0</code> from higher values: a dependency deeper than the given depth keeps its locked resolution, so <code>pnpm update --depth 0</code> updates direct dependencies only.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm run "/^build:(backend|frontend)$/"</code> selects every script whose name matches the pattern, in single-project and recursive runs alike <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322/hovercard">#13322</a>. Flags on the selector are rejected with <code>ERR_PNPM_UNSUPPORTED_SCRIPT_COMMAND_FORMAT</code>, as pnpm does.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm self-update</code> no longer takes any instruction from the project it is run in:</p> <ul> <li>pnpm is fetched through the same trusted registry and auth configuration used when switching pnpm versions, so a project <code>.npmrc</code> or <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> can no longer redirect the download or attach credentials to it, and the project's default <code>.pnpmfile.(c|m)js</code> is no longer loaded. Pnpmfiles from trusted sources (the <code>pnpmfile</code> setting, the global pnpmfile, config dependencies) still apply.</li> <li>The <code>minimumReleaseAge</code> settings in <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> no longer affect <code>self-update</code>. They still govern the project's own dependencies; for <code>self-update</code> the cooldown now comes from the built-in default, your global config, a <code>PNPM_CONFIG_*</code> environment variable, or a command-line flag. This fixes <code>self-update</code> failing inside a workspace that raises the cutoff while succeeding everywhere else, and stops a repository from either waiving the cooldown or keeping you on an outdated pnpm by raising it.</li> <li>The same applies to the <code>trustPolicy</code> settings and to <code>ci</code>: a project can no longer weaken the trust check that guards the pnpm download, nor re-enable the confirmation prompt that a CI run suppresses.</li> </ul> <p>When <code>self-update</code> refuses a version that is younger than the cutoff, an interactive run now offers to update anyway; non-interactive runs still fail. CI never prompts, even on a runner that attaches a TTY.</p> </li> </ul> <h2>Patch Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p>An aliased dependency of a protocol that resolves under its own package name — <code>jsr:</code> and the named registries — is recorded in the lockfile importer again. <code>"bar-from-jsr": "jsr:@pnpm-e2e/bar@1.0.0"</code> resolved and installed, but the importer stayed empty, so nothing reading direct dependencies out of the lockfile (<code>outdated</code>, <code>update</code>, <code>licenses</code>, dedupe, frozen-install verification) could see it <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13362" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13362/hovercard">#13362</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>An <code>allowBuilds</code> entry with the <code>set this to true or false</code> placeholder pnpm scaffolds no longer makes every command in that workspace fail with a config-parse error <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322/hovercard">#13322</a>. An undecided entry now leaves the package under the default-deny build policy, as pnpm does.</p> </li> <li> <p>Two <code>pnpm install</code> resolution fixes that made large workspaces such as <a href="https://github.com/withastro/astro">Astro</a> produce a different <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> than pnpm 11 <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13334" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13334/hovercard">#13334</a>:</p> <ul> <li>A scoped workspace package referenced through the <code>file:</code> protocol (<code>"@test/pkg": "file:./pkg"</code>) is recorded as a <code>link:</code> again instead of being copied in as a <code>file:</code> snapshot.</li> <li><code>bundledDependencies</code> / <code>bundleDependencies</code> are no longer resolved as dependencies of their own. npm ships them inside the package's tarball, so installing them again added packages the lockfile should not contain (for example <code>napi-wasm</code> under <code>@parcel/watcher-wasm</code>).</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>Executables that a package ships inside its own tarball (<code>bundledDependencies</code>) are linked again into that package's <code>node_modules/.bin</code>, under both the isolated and the hoisted node linker. A package that declares <code>bundleDependencies: true</code> instead of a list of names is now recorded in <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> the way pnpm 11 records it, and such a lockfile can be read back.</p> </li> <li> <p>Aligned <code>pnpm licenses list --json</code> package metadata and license-group ordering with the TypeScript CLI.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm --filter <package> run</code> to list the selected package's scripts and root workspace scripts when no script name is specified.</p> </li> <li> <p>Strip Unicode formatting characters from registry- and manifest-derived terminal output.</p> </li> <li> <p>Prevented dependency verification before scripts from rewriting an up-to-date lockfile.</p> </li> <li> <p>Concurrent commands in a repository that pins <code>packageManager</code> no longer race while installing the pinned pnpm version on a cold cache <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322/hovercard">#13322</a>. A task runner spawning several <code>pnpm run</code> children at once could previously fail with "failed to remove existing directory … prior to swap", or leave a child looking for a binary another process had just unlinked.</p> </li> <li> <p>Config-load warnings, such as the warning about install settings left under the <code>pnpm</code> field of <code>package.json</code>, are printed to stderr instead of stdout <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13361" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13361/hovercard">#13361</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm dedupe --check</code> now reports what deduplication would change: the importer and package snapshot diff, the <code>ERR_PNPM_DEDUPE_CHECK_ISSUES</code> error code, and the warning that points at <code>pnpm peers check</code> when the install leaves peer-dependency issues behind. <code>pnpm peers check</code> is also accepted again — the subcommand spelling used on pnpm.io and in pnpm's own dedupe output — instead of failing with "unexpected argument 'check' found" <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13321" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13321/hovercard">#13321</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A deprecated package is reported once rather than once per workspace project that depends on it, and is no longer double-counted in the "deprecated subdependencies found" summary when it is also a direct dependency <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322/hovercard">#13322</a>. Ignored build scripts are also listed with their <code>(patch_hash=…)</code> suffix, so two copies of a package that differ only by an applied patch are distinguishable.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm install --frozen-lockfile</code> no longer re-imports a varying subset of packages on every repeat install of an unchanged project <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13316" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13316/hovercard">#13316</a>. The global-virtual-store directory of a package that takes part in a dependency cycle was derived from an order that changed from run to run, so those packages landed on a fresh slot each time; it is now derived deterministically and matches the directory pnpm itself computes.</p> </li> <li> <p>When the pinned <code>packageManager</code> engine install cannot take its lock because the store cannot be written to, pnpm now reports that instead of quietly installing without the lock. A lock another process holds is unchanged — it is still waited for.</p> </li> <li> <p>Speed up installs after compatible catalog or direct dependency range changes by retaining the locked version without resolving the dependency graph again.</p> </li> <li> <p>Speed up installs after safe override changes by reusing unambiguous compatible dependency resolutions, pruning obsolete dependencies, applying independent replacements and removals together, and handling parent-scoped <code>"-"</code> overrides without full lockfile resolution.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed warm side-effects cache reuse for git dependencies.</p> </li> <li> <p>Aligned <code>pnpm dedupe --check</code> progress and error output with the TypeScript CLI.</p> </li> <li> <p>A frozen install now fails when <code>autoInstallPeers</code>, <code>dedupePeers</code>, or <code>excludeLinksFromLockfile</code> has changed since <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> was written, instead of installing against a lockfile that no longer matches the settings. The error names the drifted setting, as <code>pnpm install --frozen-lockfile</code> has always done.</p> </li> <li> <p>A repeat <code>pnpm install --frozen-lockfile</code> is a no-op again when the project has a platform-incompatible optional dependency. The skipped package is kept in <code>node_modules/.pnpm/lock.yaml</code> (<code>.modules.yaml</code> is what records the skip), so the install can once more recognize an unchanged tree instead of re-running every lifecycle and dependency build script <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13312" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13312/hovercard">#13312</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Reject frozen installs when the current pnpmfile does not match the lockfile's <code>pnpmfileChecksum</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm licenses list</code> to report dependencies from every workspace project, exclude unsupported platform packages, and mark development dependencies.</p> </li> <li> <p>Setting both <code>autoInstallPeers: false</code> and <code>dedupePeerDependents: false</code> now leaves missing peers alone, instead of still installing the ones a version elsewhere in the workspace could satisfy.</p> </li> <li> <p>Installing a local <code>file:</code> directory dependency with the global virtual store enabled no longer fails with <code>TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split')</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13335" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13335/hovercard">#13335</a>.</p> <p>Local directory dependencies — <code>file:</code> directories and injected workspace packages — now get a global-virtual-store slot of their own per project. They used to share one slot across every project that depended on a directory of the same name, so a project could end up linked to another project's copy of the dependency.</p> </li> <li> <p>A missing required peer is no longer auto-installed as a prerelease that its declared range rejects. A package peer-depending on <code>^29.0.0 || ^30.0.0</code> next to a <code>30.0.0-alpha.6</code> pulled in elsewhere in the graph now resolves a stable <code>29.x</code>/<code>30.x</code> from the registry instead of adopting the alpha <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13341" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13341/hovercard">#13341</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A lockfile entry for a git-hosted archive that records no <code>integrity</code> installs again instead of failing with <code>ERR_PNPM_MISSING_TARBALL_INTEGRITY</code>. Older pnpm versions wrote that shape for dependencies like <code>"ci-info": "watson/ci-info#f43f6a1c…"</code>, so any committed lockfile still carrying one could not be installed <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13308" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13308/hovercard">#13308</a>. The archive URL pins a full commit SHA, and pnpm fetches it without an integrity check.</p> <p>Every other remote tarball still has to carry an <code>integrity</code>, and the refusal now points at the repair: <code>pnpm clean --lockfile</code> followed by <code>pnpm install</code>.</p> <p>Error output no longer repeats the same message once per level of the internal error chain.</p> </li> <li> <p>The <code>Workspace</code> column of <code>pnpm update --interactive</code> now falls back to the project's path when its <code>name</code> is only whitespace, as it already did for a missing or empty one — all three render an equally blank label otherwise.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --interactive</code> now groups the dependencies it offers by dependency type — <code>dependencies</code>, <code>devDependencies</code>, <code>optionalDependencies</code>, <code>peerDependencies</code>, and GitHub Actions each get their own heading — and lays each group out as a column-aligned table with a <code>Package</code>/<code>Current</code>/<code>Target</code>/<code>URL</code> header, instead of one flat list.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --interactive</code> now measures its table in terminal columns rather than in characters. A package name, workspace name, or version containing wide characters (CJK, most emoji) no longer knocks its row's columns out of line with the rest of the group, and a wide character in a version no longer aborts the command with <code>Subject parameter value width cannot be greater than the container width</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13357" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13357/hovercard">#13357</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --interactive</code> run inside a workspace now shows a <code>Workspace</code> column naming the project each outdated dependency was found in, so the same package outdated in several projects can be told apart.</p> </li> <li> <p>Write single-value <code>libc</code> package metadata in the same scalar form as pnpm.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm install</code> silently skipping a local <code>file:*.tgz</code> dependency: the package is now extracted into the virtual store, recorded under <code>packages:</code> and <code>snapshots:</code>, and linked into <code>node_modules</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13379" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13379/hovercard">#13379</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A frozen install whose recorded settings no longer match the configuration — <code>overrides</code>, <code>catalogs</code>, <code>patchedDependencies</code>, and the rest — now fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH</code> naming the one setting that changed, instead of <code>ERR_PNPM_OUTDATED_LOCKFILE</code> with the whole map dumped <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322/hovercard">#13322</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm install</code> dropping a package that ships no <code>package.json</code> of its own from the lockfile. Such a package is now named after its alias and recorded at version <code>0.0.0</code> under <code>packages:</code> and <code>snapshots:</code>, and its extraction gets the placeholder <code>package.json</code> pnpm writes <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13410" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13410/hovercard">#13410</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Resolve optional peers from versions provided by local workspace packages, omit empty deprecation messages from generated lockfiles, and preserve valid lockfile pins in <code>pnpm dedupe --check</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Aligned license reports, <code>dedupe --check</code> progress and spacing, and dependency-verification output with pnpm.</p> </li> <li> <p>A <code>file:</code> dependency declared by a package that was itself installed from a local directory is now resolved relative to that package's directory, not to the importer's <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13323" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13323/hovercard">#13323</a>. Installing a project whose local dependency depends on a sibling directory (<code>file:../child</code>) no longer fails with <code>Could not install from "…" as it does not exist</code>, and the snapshot entry for such a dependency is now written as <code>file:<path></code> instead of <code><name>@file:<path></code>, matching the lockfile pnpm writes.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>npm_config_user_agent</code> now carries the configured user agent (<code>pnpm/<version> …</code>) in install lifecycle scripts, <code>pnpm run</code>, <code>pnpm exec</code>, and <code>pnpm dlx</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322/hovercard">#13322</a>. It was previously unset for install scripts and the bare string <code>pnpm</code> elsewhere, which made <code>preinstall</code> guards that check for pnpm reject the install.</p> </li> <li> <p>An auto-installed <em>optional</em> peer is no longer hoisted at a version the workspace root's own dependency on that package excludes. <code>resolvePeersFromWorkspaceRoot</code> already made the workspace root's specifier decide which version a missing <em>required</em> peer is installed at; the optional-peer picker ignored it and always took the highest version present anywhere in the graph. In a workspace whose root pins <code>postcss: 8.5.10</code>, an importer that depends on <code>webpack</code> and declares no <code>postcss</code> of its own got <code>postcss@8.5.22</code> hoisted for <code>terser-webpack-plugin</code>'s optional <code>postcss</code> peer, leaving two <code>postcss@8.5.x</code> instances in the graph <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320/hovercard">#13320</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A missing optional peer dependency is no longer satisfied by a prerelease version that its declared range doesn't accept. <code>ts-jest</code>, which declares <code>@jest/transform</code> and <code>jest-util</code> as optional peers with <code>^29.0.0 || ^30.0.0</code>, was bound to <code>30.0.0-alpha.6</code> when a <code>jest</code> 30 prerelease was elsewhere in the graph, while <code>jest</code> itself stayed on 29.</p> </li> <li> <p>With <code>autoInstallPeers: false</code>, a package's own optional peer dependencies are no longer added to its importer entry in <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> (and no longer linked into its <code>node_modules</code>) when another workspace project happens to resolve a matching version <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13325" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13325/hovercard">#13325</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>overrides</code> now also govern peers that pnpm auto-installs. Previously an override only rewrote dependencies declared in a manifest, so a peer nobody declares — installed because <code>autoInstallPeers</code> is on — resolved against its declared peer range and could bring in a second copy of the very package the override pinned. For example, with <code>overrides: { react: npm:react@19.2.0 }</code> and a lone <code>lucide-react</code> dependency, pnpm installed <code>react@18.3.1</code>; it now installs the pinned <code>react@19.2.0</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320/hovercard">#13320</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm approve-builds -g</code> is accepted again, reporting that the command is not supported with global packages rather than failing with <code>unexpected argument '-g' found</code>. <code>approve-builds</code> was the only command that declared <code>--global</code> without its <code>-g</code> short form <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13310" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13310/hovercard">#13310</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>The Rust implementation of pnpm has moved from alpha to beta releases.</p> </li> <li> <p>A catalog name containing a control character no longer corrupts <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code>. <code>pnpm add --save-catalog-name "$(printf 'a\nb')"</code> (or the same value in <code>saveCatalogName</code>) now fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_WORKSPACE_MANIFEST_WRITER_INVALID_CONTROL_CHARACTER</code> and leaves the file untouched, matching how the writer already treats <code>allowBuilds</code> and <code>overrides</code> entries.</p> </li> <li> <p>Preserve each direct dependency's locked optional peer context during <code>pnpm dedupe</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Preserve optional peer providers recorded in peer suffixes when <code>pnpm dedupe</code> rebuilds a workspace lockfile.</p> </li> <li> <p>With <code>nodeLinker: hoisted</code>, a workspace project no longer gets its own copy of a dependency whose version already won the workspace-root slot. Only the versions that lost the root slot are nested, matching the pnpm CLI. Previously every project's direct dependency was materialized under that project as well, which gave lifecycle scripts a second copy to run in.</p> </li> <li> <p>The Rust engine now warns when <code>package.json</code> still declares install settings under the <code>pnpm</code> field, which pnpm 10 moved to <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code>. A project that hasn't migrated its <code>pnpm.overrides</code> / <code>pnpm.packageExtensions</code> / <code>pnpm.patchedDependencies</code> previously saw the settings silently ignored, and only met the downstream symptom. Keys the <code>pnpm</code> field never owned are left alone.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm licenses list</code> and <code>pnpm licenses ls</code> parsing and license metadata discovery when using the global virtual store <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13332" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13332/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13332</a> and <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13333" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13333/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13333</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> that declares a package pattern whose directory does not exist yet — <code>packages/*</code> before the first package is created, say — no longer fails every command with <code>ERR_PNPM_WORKSPACE_WALK_ERROR</code>. The pattern now matches no projects, as it does in the JavaScript implementation <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13296" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13296/hovercard">#13296</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>catalog:</code> references failing to resolve when installing through a pnpr server, which errored with "No catalog entry '' was found for catalog 'default'." even though the catalog entry existed. The workspace the server reconstructs from the request has no catalog sections, so the client now sends its catalogs along with the request <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13232" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13232/hovercard">#13232</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Validate the project's pinned package manager and runtimes before running a command, matching the pnpm CLI:</p> <ul> <li>A <code>packageManager</code> / <code>devEngines.packageManager</code> pin that the running pnpm does not satisfy now fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_BAD_PM_VERSION</code> (or <code>ERR_PNPM_OTHER_PM_EXPECTED</code> when the project is pinned to another package manager), instead of being silently ignored. The check also runs under corepack, where pnpm cannot switch versions itself, and says so.</li> <li><code>devEngines.runtime</code> / <code>engines.runtime</code> entries with <code>onFail: "error"</code> or <code>onFail: "warn"</code> are validated against the Node.js, Deno, or Bun installed on the system, failing with <code>ERR_PNPM_BAD_RUNTIME_VERSION</code>.</li> <li><code>pmOnFail</code> and <code>runtimeOnFail</code> are honored as bypasses and can now be passed as <code>--pm-on-fail=<value></code> / <code>--runtime-on-fail=<value></code>, the form the error hints suggest.</li> </ul> <p>Global commands (<code>--global</code>) and commands that do not belong to the project (<code>store</code>, <code>dlx</code>, <code>self-update</code>, …) skip these checks, as does a project pin that only asked pnpm to switch versions when <code>manage-package-manager-versions</code> is turned off.</p> </li> <li> <p>Arguments after the script or command name now reach the script untouched for <code>pnpm run</code>, <code>pnpm exec</code>, <code>pnpm dlx</code>, and <code>pnpm with</code>, matching the JavaScript implementation. Previously <code>pnpm run build --config.foo=bar</code> consumed the argument as a pnpm setting instead of forwarding it, and <code>pnpm run build --silent</code> handed the script <code>--reporter=silent</code> — a token the user never typed <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13302" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13302/hovercard">#13302</a>. Put such flags before the script name (<code>pnpm run --silent build</code>) to apply them to pnpm.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed generated lockfiles to preserve packages' scalar <code>libc</code> constraints.</p> </li> <li> <p>Preserve a user-provided <code>TMPDIR</code> when scripts run with <code>unsafePerm</code> enabled; otherwise, continue using the package-local temporary directory.</p> </li> <li> <p>Added support for <code>publishConfig.name</code>, which publishes a package under a different name than the one its manifest carries in the workspace. Only the published artifact is renamed — dependents, <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code>, and release tooling keep addressing the project by its manifest name — and the new name reaches the packed manifest, the tarball filename, and everything that addresses the package at the registry: the already-published check of <code>pnpm publish -r</code>, its registry selection, and the release-planning probes of <code>pnpm change status</code> and <code>pnpm version -r</code>. This also fixes the changelog of the Rust CLI itself, which is published as <code>pnpm</code> from a workspace project named <code>pacquet</code>: its release notes were composed under the workspace name and so never made it into the published package <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13345" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13345/hovercard">#13345</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm run <script> <args></code> now forwards every argument after the script name to the script verbatim, matching the behavior of the JavaScript implementation. Previously the <code>--</code> separator was dropped, so <code>pnpm run test -- --watch</code> reached the underlying program as <code>--watch</code> and failed whenever that program claimed the option itself; arguments spelled like <code>pnpm run</code>'s own flags (<code>-s</code>, <code>--if-present</code>) were also consumed by pnpm instead of reaching the script <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13295" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13295/hovercard">#13295</a>. Pass those flags before the script name (<code>pnpm run -s test</code>) to apply them to pnpm.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm test</code>, <code>pnpm start</code>, and <code>pnpm stop</code> now forward their arguments to the script, matching the pnpm CLI. <code>pnpm test --watch</code> and <code>pnpm start --port 3000</code> previously failed with a usage error, and <code>pnpm stop</code> claimed <code>--if-present</code> and <code>-s</code> for itself instead of passing them on. As with <code>pnpm run</code>, every token after the command name reaches the script verbatim, a <code>--</code> separator included.</p> </li> <li> <p>Added the <code>--workspace-root</code> (<code>-w</code>) flag, which runs the command on the root workspace project. <code>pnpm add -D typescript prettier -w</code> from a workspace subdirectory now saves to the root <code>package.json</code> instead of failing with "unexpected argument '-w' found" <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13031" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13031/hovercard">#13031</a>. Combined with <code>--recursive</code>, the flag narrows the run to the root project alone. <code>-w</code> may not be used together with <code>--global</code>, and may only be used inside a workspace.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>patchedDependencies</code> patch files that pnpm applies no longer fail with <code>ERR_PNPM_PATCH_FAILED</code>: a hunk whose last line is context in a file with no final newline, and an LF patch against a CRLF file, both apply again <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13322/hovercard">#13322</a>. A hunk that has drifted from its recorded line numbers is also retried nearby, matching pnpm.</p> </li> <li> <p>A peer dependency is now recorded in the lockfile at the version and peer suffix the peer provider actually resolved to. Peers whose provider carried peer suffixes of its own could be recorded against a package instance that no importer installs, leaving an unreachable entry in <code>snapshots:</code> and a peer bound to the wrong instance <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320/hovercard">#13320</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A peer dependency that the workspace root already provides is no longer installed a second time. With <code>resolvePeersFromWorkspaceRoot</code> enabled (the default), a missing peer is matched against the <strong>workspace root</strong> project's dependencies; it was matched against the dependencies of whichever project was being resolved, so a project that didn't declare the peer itself resolved its own copy from the registry. In <a href="https://github.com/vercel/next.js">vercel/next.js</a>, whose <code>overrides</code> pin <code>react</code> to a single canary build, this pulled in a second <code>react</code> and paired it with <code>react-dom</code> from the canary — a combination the pin exists to prevent.</p> </li> <li> <p>Under <code>resolvePeersFromWorkspaceRoot</code>, a workspace root dependency declared with <code>link:</code> or <code>file:</code> (or the path form of <code>workspace:</code>, such as <code>workspace:../pkg</code>) now satisfies another project's missing peer dependency at the linked package's own version, instead of being hoisted as a path. Those specifiers are relative to the project that declares them, so the same specifier reached a different directory — or none — from the project the peer was hoisted into, leaving a broken link. The root now has the same authority over the peer as it has when it declares the package with a version range <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13373" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13373/hovercard">#13373</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Two <code>pnpm install</code> peer-resolution fixes that made large workspaces such as <a href="https://github.com/withastro/astro">Astro</a> produce a different <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> than pnpm 11 <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13334" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13334/hovercard">#13334</a>:</p> <ul> <li>A package that declares the same name in both <code>dependencies</code> and <code>peerDependencies</code> no longer gets a nested copy of it when the parent already supplies that name, which is what pnpm does with <code>autoInstallPeers</code> disabled. The nested copy hid the peer, so the package was recorded without the peer context it resolves in.</li> <li>A duplicate peer-suffixed variant that collapses into a larger, compatible one now collapses everywhere it is referenced. A variant kept alive by a single consumer's edge no longer lingers in the lockfile.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>Closed the remaining gaps in how unscoped per-registry <code>.npmrc</code> settings are pinned to the registry their own source file declared:</p> <ul> <li>An inline <code>cert=</code> / <code>key=</code> written with <code>\n</code> escapes now expands to a real multi-line PEM, matching the URL-scoped <code>//host/:cert=</code> spelling.</li> <li><code>pnpm config get</code> / <code>pnpm config list</code> now report a rescoped credential under the URL-scoped key it was pinned to, instead of the unscoped key it was written as.</li> <li>The deprecation warning names the file it read and lists every setting it pinned, including <code>tokenHelper</code>.</li> <li>A credential with no registry of its own is no longer attached to the resolved default registry, which repository config can move. The same rule now covers the <code>@pnpm/napi</code> bindings: the <code>authHeaderByUri</code> entry written with an empty (<code>""</code>) key is pinned to the <code>registry</code> / <code>registries.default</code> the host passed alongside it, never to a registry the project's <code>.npmrc</code> names.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p>The projects that run their own lifecycle scripts (<code>preinstall</code>, <code>install</code>, <code>postinstall</code>, <code>prepare</code>, …) now match pnpm in every install-family command. A project runs them when the command installs it in full, and — in a workspace the command only partly covers — whenever the command mutates it at all; the workspace root runs them even when the command was pointed at another project, because it is installed in full alongside it. As a result, <code>pnpm update <pkg></code> and <code>pnpm add <pkg></code> in a workspace no longer skip the workspace root's scripts, <code>pnpm update</code> at a workspace root no longer runs the other members' scripts, and <code>pnpm update --latest</code> no longer runs the project's own scripts (it rewrites named dependency specs, so it is a partial install like <code>pnpm update <pkg></code>) <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13358" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13358/hovercard">#13358</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Print the script command by default when running a filtered lifecycle script. The command remains hidden with <code>--silent</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Run dependency verification consistently after regenerating a lockfile with <code>dedupePeers</code> enabled.</p> </li> <li> <p>Aligned the <code>hoistedDependencies</code> contents and ordering in <code>node_modules/.modules.yaml</code> with pnpm.</p> </li> <li> <p>Preserve whether package <code>libc</code> metadata uses a string or an array when writing the lockfile.</p> </li> <li> <p>A <code>package.json</code> that starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark is read again instead of failing with <code>expected value at line 1 column 1</code>. Workspace discovery, dependency manifests (including bin linking), tarball extraction, and <code>pnpm publish</code> of a pre-built tarball all accept one, matching pnpm <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13311" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13311/hovercard">#13311</a>. A manifest that really is malformed now reports its path in the error.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>ERR_PNPM_BROKEN_LOCKFILE</code> when installing with a pnpm 10 lockfile that has a <code>patchedDependencies</code> section. See <a class="issue-link js-issue-link" data-error-text="Failed to load title" data-id="4975396672" data-permission-text="Title is private" data-url="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13307" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13307/hovercard" href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13307">#13307</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm -r run "/pattern/" --no-bail</code> no longer exits zero when one of a project's matched scripts fails and a later one passes. The run summary carries a single status per project, and the passing script overwrote the recorded failure.</p> </li> <li> <p>Resolution failures now report the error pnpm defines for them. A well-formed range that the registry publishes nothing for fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_NO_MATCHING_VERSION</code> — naming the latest release, the other dist-tags, and the <code>pnpm view <pkg> versions</code> command that lists the rest — instead of <code>ERR_PNPM_SPEC_NOT_SUPPORTED_BY_ANY_RESOLVER</code>. A package the registry doesn't have fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_FETCH_404</code> and the "not in the npm registry, or you have no permission to fetch it" hint (plus which authorization header was sent, since a private registry often answers a permission failure with a 404) instead of a bare HTTP-client message. A wrapper that quotes its cause verbatim no longer prints the same sentence twice in the error report.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm add <workspace-package></code> to resolve the local package when <code>linkWorkspacePackages</code> is enabled.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>$dep-name</code> self-references in <code>overrides</code> are now resolved against the root manifest's direct dependencies, so an override such as <code>rolldown: $rolldown</code> records the concrete specifier in <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> and no longer fails a frozen install with <code>ERR_PNPM_OUTDATED_LOCKFILE</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13314" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13314/hovercard">#13314</a>. A reference to a package that is not a direct dependency fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_CANNOT_RESOLVE_OVERRIDE_VERSION</code>, and the deprecated syntax now warns, pointing at catalogs.</p> </li> <li> <p>The root project's <code>pnpm:devPreinstall</code> script now runs before resolution and linking, as it does in pnpm 11. It is skipped under <code>--ignore-scripts</code>, <code>--lockfile-only</code> and <code>--dry-run</code>, by <code>pnpm fetch</code> and <code>pnpm rebuild</code>, and by a repeat install that is already up to date. Workspaces that use the hook to prepare state the install depends on — such as <a href="https://github.com/vercel/next.js">next.js</a>, which generates a placeholder <code>next</code> bin with it — were left with dependents linked against files that were never created <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13313" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13313/hovercard">#13313</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>The lockfile-verification line now dates a cached verdict — <code>✓ Lockfile passes supply-chain policies (verified 253ms ago)</code> — instead of the timeless <code>(previously verified)</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315/hovercard">#13315</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm install</code>, <code>run</code>, <code>test</code>, <code>update</code>, <code>remove</code>, <code>link</code>, <code>unlink</code>, <code>prune</code>, and <code>rebuild</code> now print the workspace scope they resolved — <code>Scope: all 41 workspace projects</code>, or <code>Scope: 5 of 41 workspace projects</code> under a <code>--filter</code>. This is the confirmation that a filter selected what was intended <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315/hovercard">#13315</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>An install that blocks a dependency's build scripts now appends a placeholder for it to <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code>, so approving or denying the build is an edit rather than writing the block by hand:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-yaml notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="allowBuilds: es5-ext: set this to true or false"><pre><span class="pl-ent">allowBuilds</span>: <span class="pl-ent">es5-ext</span>: <span class="pl-s">set this to true or false</span></pre></div> <p>A placeholder is not a decision — the build stays blocked until it is replaced with <code>true</code> or <code>false</code> — and an existing entry is never overwritten <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315/hovercard">#13315</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>--parallel</code> being treated as the script name when placed before <code>run</code> in a recursive command.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>scriptShell</code> now selects the shell for lifecycle scripts too — dependency build scripts and a project's own <code>preinstall</code>/<code>install</code>/<code>postinstall</code>/<code>prepare</code> and <code>pnpm:devPreinstall</code> — not only for <code>pnpm run</code> and <code>pnpm exec</code>. A workspace that configures a shell was still getting the platform default (<code>sh</code> / <code>cmd</code>) for everything the install itself spawns.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>shamefullyHoist: true</code> to create public root dependency links.</p> </li> <li> <p>Prevented optional peers from being selected from an unrelated workspace package's shared dependency context.</p> </li> <li> <p>The store index now keys URL, git-host, and <code>type: git</code> dependencies by their bare resolution id, matching the key pnpm 11 writes <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13365" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13365/hovercard">#13365</a>. Previously these rows carried a <code><name>@</code> prefix, so a store warmed by one pnpm major was cold for the other and every non-registry dependency was re-downloaded, re-extracted, and re-imported on a switch. A remote tarball also occupied two index rows instead of one, doubling its extraction work.</p> </li> <li> <p>A project that pins pnpm through <code>devEngines.packageManager</code> (or a v12+ <code>packageManager</code> field) now gets its <code>packageManagerDependencies</code> recorded in <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code> by every command, not just by the install-family ones <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13348" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13348/hovercard">#13348</a>. Running <code>pnpm list</code> (or any other command) in a freshly cloned project no longer leaves the lockfile without the pinned version. The <code>pmOnFail</code> setting now also decides whether the pin is recorded: <code>--pm-on-fail=ignore</code> keeps it out of the lockfile even when the manifest asks for a stricter policy, and vice versa.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm licenses list</code> to detect licenses from license files and preserve the latest package version's development classification.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --latest</code> now rewrites <code>jsr:</code> dependencies. The manifest keeps the protocol and the range operator it declared, so <code>jsr:1.0.0</code> becomes <code>jsr:2.0.0</code> and <code>jsr:@scope/name@^1.0.0</code> becomes <code>jsr:@scope/name@^2.0.0</code>, instead of being left at the old version <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13363" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13363/hovercard">#13363</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --latest</code> now rewrites dependencies using a named registry alias. The manifest keeps the alias prefix and the range operator it declared, so <code>gh:1.0.0</code> becomes <code>gh:2.0.0</code> and <code>gh:@acme/foo@^1.0.0</code> becomes <code>gh:@acme/foo@^2.0.0</code>, instead of being left at the old version <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13393" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13393/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13393</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Breaking change from pnpm v11.</strong> Under <code>engineStrict</code>, an install fails when an incompatible package is reached through a regular <code>dependencies</code> edge of an installable package, even when that whole subtree hangs off an <code>optionalDependencies</code> entry. pnpm v11 installs the package and emits an install-check warning instead. Packages reachable only through optional edges, or through a package that was itself skipped, are still skipped in both versions <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13286" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13286/hovercard">#13286</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>A lockfile entry whose tarball resolution records no <code>integrity</code> is now reported by the lockfile-verification gate, before anything is downloaded: every offending entry is listed in one <code>ERR_PNPM_MISSING_TARBALL_INTEGRITY</code> error instead of failing the install one fetch at a time after the gate had already passed the lockfile <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13364" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13364/hovercard">#13364</a>. An <code>integrity: ''</code> that pins nothing is treated the same as a missing one, and the exemption for git-host archive URLs is now read from the URL rather than the lockfile's own <code>gitHosted</code> marker.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm licenses list</code> to read licenses from legacy package manifest fields.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>--workspace-root</code> (<code>-w</code>) selecting the current workspace when <code>--dir</code> pointed at a nonexistent directory outside it (for example <code>pnpm --dir ../../elsewhere add -w foo</code>). The command now fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_NOT_IN_WORKSPACE</code>, matching pnpm. A nonexistent <code>--dir</code> inside the workspace still resolves to the workspace root as before.</p> </li> </ul>

## [@vercel/python-runtime@0.17.0](https://github.com/vercel/vercel/releases/tag/%40vercel%2Fpython-runtime%400.17.0)
*GitHub Releases · Vercel CLI* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.70
Tags: api_update, developer_tool, cli_tool, tool_update

> <h3>Minor Changes</h3> <ul> <li> <p><a class="commit-link" data-hovercard-type="commit" data-hovercard-url="https://github.com/vercel/vercel/commit/17ee73663e30c0ddd91cdf5fcf134c55a0a6ea0a/hovercard" href="https://github.com/vercel/vercel/commit/17ee73663e30c0ddd91cdf5fcf134c55a0a6ea0a"><tt>17ee736</tt></a>: Replace the vercel-workers integration for Python queue subscribers and workflows with the new vercel-queue SDK:</p> <ul> <li><code>[[tool.vercel.subscribers]]</code> entrypoints are introspected at build time via <code>vercel.queue.get_subscriptions()</code> and served through generated <code>vercel.queue.asgi_app()</code> handler modules, with <code>queue/v2beta</code> triggers carrying the SDK-registered consumer groups and per-subscription tuning.</li> <li>Celery and Dramatiq projects get the matching <code>vercel-celery</code>/<code>vercel-dramatiq</code> integration package injected automatically (bundled variant unless <code>vercel-queue</code> is an explicit dependency), in builds and in <code>vercel dev</code>.</li> <li><code>[[tool.vercel.workflows]]</code> entrypoints follow the SDK generation: projects on <code>vercel</code> >= 0.8.0 are served through vercel-queue like subscribers; older or undeterminable versions keep the legacy vercel-workers serving (worker env markers, injected pinned <code>vercel-workers</code>).</li> <li>Projects that depend on <code>vercel-workers</code> directly keep the legacy integration wholesale: legacy subscriber schema, direct entrypoint serving, worker env markers.</li> <li><code>vercel dev</code> serves queue sidecars through <code>vercel.queue.asgi_app()</code> for new-SDK projects, and its queue broker delivers with the SDK-registered consumer groups introspected at sidecar startup (matching production trigger behavior); legacy projects keep the vercel-workers bootstrap.</li> <li>The CLI no longer injects <code>config.hasWorkerServices</code>; the Python builder makes all queue-serving decisions from project metadata.</li> </ul> </li> </ul>

href="https://github.com/vercel/vercel/commit/0f04613672fa3ef05e77df519ceb1d7eafacc486"><tt>0f04613</tt></a>: Add <code>vercel vcr permissions</code> subcommands for managing which teams can pull images from a VCR repository: <code>vcr permissions <repository> ls</code> lists teams with access (by team slug), <code>add</code> and <code>rm</code> grant or revoke access for one or more teams (comma-separated team ids or slugs), and <code>clear</code> removes access for every team.</p> </li> <li> <p><a class="commit-link" data-hovercard-type="commit" data-hovercard-url="https://github.com/vercel/vercel/commit/17ee73663e30c0ddd91cdf5fcf134c55a0a6ea0a/hovercard" href="https://github.com/vercel/vercel/commit/17ee73663e30c0ddd91cdf5fcf134c55a0a6ea0a"><tt>17ee736</tt></a>: Replace the vercel-workers integration for Python queue subscribers and workflows with the new vercel-queue SDK:</p> <ul> <li><code>[[tool.vercel.subscribers]]</code> entrypoints are introspected at build time via <code>vercel.queue.get_subscriptions()</code> and served through generated <code>vercel.queue.asgi_app()</code> handler modules, with <code>queue/v2beta</code> triggers carrying the SDK-registered consumer groups and per-subscription tuning.</li> <li>Celery and Dramatiq projects get the matching <code>vercel-celery</code>/<code>vercel-dramatiq</code> integration package injected automatically (bundled variant unless <code>vercel-queue</code> is an explicit dependency), in builds and in <code>vercel dev</code>.</li> <li><code>[[tool.vercel.workflows]]</code> entrypoints follow the SDK generation: projects on <code>vercel</code> >= 0.8.0 are served through vercel-queue like subscribers; older or undeterminable versions keep the legacy vercel-workers serving (worker env markers, injected pinned <code>vercel-workers</code>).</li> <li>Projects that depend on <code>vercel-workers</code> directly keep the legacy integration wholesale: legacy subscriber schema, direct entrypoint serving, worker env markers.</li> <li><code>vercel dev</code> serves queue sidecars through <code>vercel.queue.asgi_app()</code> for new-SDK projects, and its queue broker delivers with the SDK-registered consumer groups introspected at sidecar startup (matching production trigger behavior); legacy projects keep the vercel-workers bootstrap.</li> <li>The CLI no longer injects <code>config.hasWorkerServices</code>; the Python builder makes all queue-serving decisions from project metadata.</li> </ul> </li> <li> <p><a class="commit-link" data-hovercard-type="commit" ## [pnpm 11.18](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v11.18.0)
*GitHub Releases · pnpm* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.70
Tags: developer_tool, cli_tool, tool_update

> <h2>Minor Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p>Fixed an installed optional dependency being left without one of its own required dependencies. When a package reached through <code>optionalDependencies</code> is installable on the current system but one of its regular <code>dependencies</code> is not, a lockfile-based install skipped that dependency and installed the parent anyway, so importing the parent failed with <code>MODULE_NOT_FOUND</code>. The dependency is now installed, and an install-check warning reports the incompatibility. A dependency is still only skipped when every path to it is optional, or when the package that pulls it in was itself skipped <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13286" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13286/hovercard">#13286</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm setup</code> now appends <code>PNPM_HOME</code> and the global bin directory to the GitHub Actions environment files (<code>GITHUB_ENV</code> and <code>GITHUB_PATH</code>), so later steps in the same job can run <code>pnpm add --global</code> and other global commands <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/9191" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/9191/hovercard">#9191</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Added support for <code>publishConfig.name</code>, which publishes a package under a different name than the one its manifest carries in the workspace. It is for a project whose published name is already taken by a sibling project, which otherwise has to be renamed by a build step just before publishing. Only the published artifact is renamed — dependents, <code>pnpm-lock.yaml</code>, and release tooling keep addressing the project by its manifest name — and the new name reaches the packed manifest, the tarball filename, and everything that addresses the package at the registry: the already-published check of <code>pnpm publish -r</code>, its registry selection, and the release-planning probes of <code>pnpm change status</code> and <code>pnpm version -r</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13345" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13345/hovercard">#13345</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm self-update</code> no longer takes any instruction from the project it is run in:</p> <ul> <li>pnpm is fetched through the same trusted registry and auth configuration used when switching pnpm versions, so a project <code>.npmrc</code> or <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> can no longer redirect the download or attach credentials to it, and the project's default <code>.pnpmfile.(c|m)js</code> is no longer loaded. Pnpmfiles from trusted sources (the <code>pnpmfile</code> setting, the global pnpmfile, config dependencies) still apply.</li> <li>The <code>minimumReleaseAge</code> settings in <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code> no longer affect <code>self-update</code>. They still govern the project's own dependencies; for <code>self-update</code> the cooldown now comes from the built-in default, your global config, a <code>PNPM_CONFIG_*</code> environment variable, or a command-line flag. This fixes <code>self-update</code> failing inside a workspace that raises the cutoff while succeeding everywhere else, and stops a repository from either waiving the cooldown or keeping you on an outdated pnpm by raising it.</li> <li>The same applies to the <code>trustPolicy</code> settings and to <code>ci</code>: a project can no longer weaken the trust check that guards the pnpm download, nor re-enable the confirmation prompt that a CI run suppresses.</li> </ul> <p>When <code>self-update</code> refuses a version that is younger than the cutoff, an interactive run now offers to update anyway; non-interactive runs still fail. CI never prompts, even on a runner that attaches a TTY.</p> </li> </ul> <h2>Patch Changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm licenses list</code> to report every version when the same package is installed under multiple aliases <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13438" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13438/hovercard">pnpm/pnpm#13438</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Sort <code>pnpm dedupe --check</code> snapshot changes for stable output across pnpm implementations.</p> </li> <li> <p>Strip Unicode formatting characters from registry- and manifest-derived terminal output.</p> </li> <li> <p>Speed up installs after compatible catalog or direct dependency range changes by retaining the locked version without resolving the dependency graph again.</p> </li> <li> <p>Speed up installs after safe override changes by reusing unambiguous compatible dependency resolutions, pruning obsolete dependencies, applying independent replacements and removals together, and handling parent-scoped <code>"-"</code> overrides without full lockfile resolution.</p> </li> <li> <p>Installing a local <code>file:</code> directory dependency with the global virtual store enabled no longer fails with <code>TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split')</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13335" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13335/hovercard">#13335</a>.</p> <p>Local directory dependencies — <code>file:</code> directories and injected workspace packages — now get a global-virtual-store slot of their own per project. They used to share one slot across every project that depended on a directory of the same name, so a project could end up linked to another project's copy of the dependency.</p> </li> <li> <p>The <code>Workspace</code> column of <code>pnpm update --interactive</code> now falls back to the project's path when its <code>name</code> is only whitespace, as it already did for a missing or empty one — all three render an equally blank label otherwise.</p> </li> <li> <p>Checking GitHub Actions dependencies for updates is now opt-in for every command. Neither <code>pnpm outdated</code> nor <code>pnpm update</code> reads the workflow files unless <code>--include-github-actions</code> is passed or <code>update.githubActions</code> is set to <code>true</code> in <code>pnpm-workspace.yaml</code>. Reading them runs <code>git ls-remote</code> against every referenced repository, which fails in environments where GitHub is not reachable the way pnpm assumes (a GitHub Enterprise Server, a custom certificate authority, or an offline network) <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13254" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13254/hovercard">#13254</a>.</p> <p><code>pnpm outdated</code> accepts the <code>--include-github-actions</code> option too.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --interactive</code> now measures its table in terminal columns rather than in characters. A package name, workspace name, or version containing wide characters (CJK, most emoji) no longer knocks its row's columns out of line with the rest of the group, and a wide character in a version no longer aborts the command with <code>Subject parameter value width cannot be greater than the container width</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13357" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13357/hovercard">#13357</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>The <code>Workspace</code> column of <code>pnpm update --interactive</code> is more informative in two cases. A dependency outdated at the same version in several workspace projects is offered as one choice, since selecting it updates every project — that choice now names all of them instead of only the first. And a workspace project without a <code>name</code> is now labelled with its path rather than left blank, so several unnamed projects can be told apart.</p> </li> <li> <p>An auto-installed <em>optional</em> peer is no longer hoisted at a version the workspace root's own dependency on that package excludes. <code>resolvePeersFromWorkspaceRoot</code> already made the workspace root's specifier decide which version a missing <em>required</em> peer is installed at; the optional-peer picker ignored it and always took the highest version present anywhere in the graph. In a workspace whose root pins <code>postcss: 8.5.10</code>, an importer that depends on <code>webpack</code> and declares no <code>postcss</code> of its own got <code>postcss@8.5.22</code> hoisted for <code>terser-webpack-plugin</code>'s optional <code>postcss</code> peer, leaving two <code>postcss@8.5.x</code> instances in the graph <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320/hovercard">#13320</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>overrides</code> now also govern peers that pnpm auto-installs. Previously an override only rewrote dependencies declared in a manifest, so a peer nobody declares — installed because <code>autoInstallPeers</code> is on — resolved against its declared peer range and could bring in a second copy of the very package the override pinned. For example, with <code>overrides: { react: npm:react@19.2.0 }</code> and a lone <code>lucide-react</code> dependency, pnpm installed <code>react@18.3.1</code>; it now installs the pinned <code>react@19.2.0</code> <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13320/hovercard">#13320</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Under <code>resolvePeersFromWorkspaceRoot</code>, a workspace root dependency declared with <code>link:</code> or <code>file:</code> (or the path form of <code>workspace:</code>, such as <code>workspace:../pkg</code>) now satisfies another project's missing peer dependency at the linked package's own version, instead of being hoisted as a path. Those specifiers are relative to the project that declares them, so the same specifier reached a different directory — or none — from the project the peer was hoisted into, leaving a broken link. The root now has the same authority over the peer as it has when it declares the package with a version range <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13373" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13373/hovercard">#13373</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Installs through a pnpr server now apply the project's whole verification policy. <code>minimumReleaseAgeExclude</code>, <code>minimumReleaseAgeIgnoreMissingTime</code>, <code>trustPolicy</code>, <code>trustPolicyExclude</code>, <code>trustPolicyIgnoreAfter</code>, and <code>trustLockfile</code> were ignored, so excluded packages were still held back and a lockfile containing them could be rejected.</p> <p><code>trustPolicy: no-downgrade</code> no longer fails with <code>TRUST_POLICY_INCOMPATIBLE_WITH_PNPR</code> when a pnpr server is configured.</p> <p><code>--frozen-lockfile</code> and <code>--no-prefer-frozen-lockfile</code> are now honored on the pnpr path, instead of resolving and rewriting the lockfile anyway. Since <code>frozenLockfile</code> defaults to <code>true</code> on CI, a CI install through a pnpr server now fails on an out-of-date lockfile rather than updating it.</p> </li> <li> <p>Workspace installs through a pnpr server no longer crash with <code>Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'filter')</code> after linking, when <code>minimumReleaseAge</code> is active <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13275" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13275/hovercard">#13275</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Fixed <code>pnpm dedupe</code> updating valid catalog resolutions when another matching version exists in the lockfile.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm -r run "/pattern/" --no-bail</code> no longer exits zero when one of a project's matched scripts fails and a later one passes. The run summary carries a single status per project, and the passing script overwrote the recorded failure.</p> </li> <li> <p>Restored the store block a first install prints, naming how packages were materialized and where the stores live <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13315/hovercard">#13315</a>:</p> <div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="Packages are hard linked from the content-addressable store to the virtual store. Content-addressable store is at: ~/.local/share/pnpm/store/v11 Virtual store is at: node_modules/.pnpm"><pre lang="text" class="notranslate"><code>Packages are hard linked from the content-addressable store to the virtual store. Content-addressable store is at: ~/.local/share/pnpm/store/v11 Virtual store is at: node_modules/.pnpm </code></pre></div> </li> <li> <p>The root project's <code>pnpm:devPreinstall</code> script now runs before resolution and linking, as it does in pnpm 11. It is skipped under <code>--ignore-scripts</code>, <code>--lockfile-only</code> and <code>--dry-run</code>, by <code>pnpm fetch</code> and <code>pnpm rebuild</code>, and by a repeat install that is already up to date. Workspaces that use the hook to prepare state the install depends on — such as <a href="https://github.com/vercel/next.js">next.js</a>, which generates a placeholder <code>next</code> bin with it — were left with dependents linked against files that were never created <a href="https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13313" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/pnpm/pnpm/issues/13313/hovercard">#13313</a>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Prevented <code>pnpm dedupe --check</code> from removing an incompatible <code>node_modules</code> directory.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>pnpm update --workspace</code> no longer links dependencies the user never named:</p> <ul> <li>Running it with <code>updateConfig.ignoreDependencies</code> configured no longer fails with <code>ERR_PNPM_WORKSPACE_PACKAGE_NOT_FOUND</code> for a dependency that is only published to the registry. Such dependencies keep their specifiers, as they already did when no dependencies were ignored.</li> <li>Passing package selectors that match no direct dependency no longer falls back to linking every workspace dependency.</li> </ul> </li> </ul> <h2>Platinum Sponsors</h2> <table> <tbody> <tr> <td align="center" valign="middle"> <a ## [What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26935v1)
*arXiv CS.AI* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.90
Tags: developer_tool, agent_tool

> Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot. This assumption breaks when AI agents browse the web through browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary classifiers structurally cannot represent. We present a three-class detection framework distinguishing humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector misroutes agent sessions because its label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%; adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in all 30 runs (3 model families $\times$ 10 seeds). To measure evasion resistance, we construct a five-level evasion ladder spanning passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data ($n = 2299$ evasion sessions). Across 10 seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22990 per-seed predictions. The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces, and this absence signature survives trajectory manipulation. Exhaustive search over all feature subsets of size 1-5 (9401 GBMs) shows that two behavioral features (mouse_event_rate, teleport_click_ratio) give 100% observed agent recall at every evasion level with agent precision 0.994; five features lift macro-F1 to 0.991. The signal is redundantly encoded: removing teleport_click_ratio leaves agent detection at 100%. The single-feature regime is degenerate, flagging every agent only by collapsing the classifier to always predict "agent". Two features robustly isolate agents; five separate all three traffic classes at macro-F1 $\geq 0.99$.

## [Desktop-Delta Bench: Do Computer-Use Models Understand Desktop GUI Transitions?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26041v1)
*arXiv CS.AI* | 28/07/2026 | Score: 0.90
Tags: open_source, agent_tool

> Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act through desktop GUIs to complete long-horizon tasks. Current benchmarks primarily measure end-task success or single-frame grounding. Neither isolates whether a model can reconstruct the causal, task-relevant transition produced by an action- crucial for rejecting stale observations, verifying progress, and recovering from failure. This is difficult because inference, remote input, app rendering, and screenshot capture are asynchronous: the next observation may be delayed, occluded, transient, or unrelated, then misread as progress and carried into subsequent planning. We introduce Desktop-Delta Bench (DDB), an offline step-level benchmark with 2,013 human-verified instances from novel, multi-app Linux trajectories across ~15 applications and 50 task domains. DDB trajectories targets 3 failure dimensions- state verification, source tracking, and context-aware control- through 2 complementary tasks: 463 3-frame temporal-ordering instances, including 105 with a cross-trajectory decoy, and 1,550 before-after pairs labeled from 5 actions + its payload. We evaluate 8 closed and open-source model families across 32 ordering and 16 single-action settings, observing consistent gaps. Ordering remains unsaturated: best non-decoy and decoy exact-match rates are 65.1% and 65.7%. Task context improves decoy identification by 6.9 percentage points but reduces non-decoy exact match by 2.2 points; error analysis reveals systematic copying of the presented A-B-C order. Single-action results show that inferring the action family is harder than locating it: click F1 is 0.96 vs, 0.76 for drag, while recognized drags are generally localized well. DDB, thus, complements end-to-end benchmarks by filling the missing diagnostic layer between GUI grounding and final task success, enabling targeted improvements to desktop CUA verification, reliability, and recovery.

## [Penelope: Localized Latent Recurrence for Efficient Structured Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25915v1)
*arXiv CS.AI* | 28/07/2026 | Score: 0.90
Tags: open_source, developer_tool

> Complex structured reasoning tasks often require additional computation, yet current language models obtain it mainly by increasing parameter scale or by serializing intermediate steps as chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens. The former raises training and deployment costs, while the latter ties reasoning computation to autoregressive output length. We introduce Penelope, an efficient latent-reasoning framework for pretrained decoder-only Transformers that localizes recurrent computation to a selected decoder interval. The lower decoder prefix is evaluated once to construct a problem-conditioned boundary memory, which is then iteratively refined through time-modulated GRU dynamics and recurrent readout states before answer generation. A progressive CoT-to-latent curriculum transfers visible reasoning into this internal recurrent path, allowing additional computation to be allocated in latent space without repeatedly executing the complete decoder or generating a long intermediate trace. Experiments on open-source structured-reasoning benchmarks show that, at validation-selected latent budgets, Penelope attains competitive accuracy relative to established latent-reasoning models while reducing measured inference latency. These results show that latent refinement can be localized to a narrow decoder interval, reducing repeated full-decoder execution without generating a long visible reasoning trace and providing a practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for decoder-only Transformer models.

## [Toward Standardized Cross-Vendor Agent Tool Trust Management in Autonomous Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25914v1)
*arXiv CS.AI* | 28/07/2026 | Score: 0.90
Tags: developer_tool, agent_tool

> Autonomous Network Levels 4-5 require AI agents to invoke tools across vendor boundaries without human oversight, yet existing management standards lack a standardized mechanism for cross-vendor trust visibility. When a tool from Vendor B is compromised, agents from Vendor A continue invoking it -- unaware of the trust degradation -- causing cascading service impact. We present AgentToolMO, a proposed 3GPP NRM information model for agent tool trust management. The model comprises: a formally defined trust state machine with provable graduated enforcement, damped cascade propagation with bounded convergence, cross-vendor trust notifications via existing Management Services (MnS) interfaces, and retroactive impact assessment through NRM dependency graph traversal. Simulation-based evaluation across multi-vendor topologies shows that standardized cross-vendor notifications reduce blast radius from hours-scale undetected propagation to near-real-time containment bounded by MnS notification delivery, with cascade convergence guaranteed in bounded iterations and sub-linear notification scaling across vendor domains. The framework operates within existing 3GPP management infrastructure, leverages existing protocols, and provides a standardization pathway for trustworthy multi-vendor autonomous network management.

## [Linguistic Monoculture in LLM-Assisted Language Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27134v1)
*arXiv CS.AI* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.82
Tags: developer_tool, tool_update

> Writing and communication are increasingly mediated by large language models (LLMs) that are being used to draft, revise and polish text. Although such assistance can improve clarity and help authors meet institutional expectations, widespread reliance on shared models may reduce population-level variation in linguistic form, a phenomenon we refer to as linguistic monoculture. We develop a mathematical framework in which authors and LLMs are represented as distributions over linguistic features and coevolve through repeated interaction. We analyze three interaction mechanisms: a shared model with a fixed linguistic distribution, a shared model recursively updated from author outputs, and personalized models updated through author-specific and population-level feedback. We characterize the resulting equilibria and convergence rates, showing that, shared models can drive authors toward a common norm, recursive feedback relocates the shared norm without altering pairwise spread under common conformity, and personalization can preserve a family of distinct author-model equilibria with nonzero linguistic diversity. We then endogenize conformity as a strategic choice trading off private benefits from clarity, legibility, and perceived fluency against distinctive style. Within this utility model, individually rational authors may conform more than is socially optimal because they do not internalize the value their distinctiveness provides to others, creating a negative externality and a price of monoculture that is finite for each fixed instance but can grow without bound when distinctiveness dominates authenticity. Synthetic simulations illustrate how fixed shared assistance, recursive feedback, and personalization produce different long-run diversity outcomes.

## [Skillful forecasting of offshore winds from satellite scatterometer constellations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27152v1)
*arXiv CS.LG* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: developer_tool, tool_update

> Accurate intraday forecasts of offshore wind are becoming increasingly important for power system operation and the integration of growing shares of offshore wind energy. Operational forecasts rely predominantly on numerical weather prediction (NWP), which is not optimized for lead times of minutes to hours, where initial-condition accuracy dominates forecast skill. Although satellite scatterometer observations are routinely assimilated into NWP, they have not previously been used directly for forecasting. Here we present WindCastNet, the first satellite-based nowcasting framework for offshore wind speed and direction, introducing a new paradigm for intraday forecasting that learns from spatiotemporally irregular satellite observations. WindCastNet predicts offshore wind fields from observations acquired by satellite scatterometer constellations. WindCastNet employs a partial convolutional long short-term memory network that exploits microwave radar observations from the European, Chinese, and Indian scatterometers despite their irregular spatial coverage, asynchronous sampling, and variable revisit times. Spatial observation masks and inter-observation intervals are encoded, while a continuous temporal representation enables forecasts at arbitrary lead times. Evaluated over the North Sea, WindCastNet reduces the root-mean-square error by 23% and 7% relative to the HARMONIE MEPS model at lead times of 1 and 2 h, respectively, and outperforms persistence by 9-15% during the first three forecast hours. Forecast skill decreases under strong-wind conditions and spatially non-uniform flow. These results demonstrate that satellite scatterometer constellations can provide an independent and competitive source of short-term offshore wind forecasts, opening new opportunities for renewable energy forecasting but also broader marine weather applications, including tropical cyclone nowcasting.

## [MindForge: Teaching Small Language Models Whole-Life-Cycle Software Engineering via Source-Free Program Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27146v1)
*arXiv CS.LG* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: open_source, cli_tool

> Coding agents have made substantial progress on software engineering tasks that modify existing codebases, including bug fixing and feature implementation. However, constructing a complete program from scratch remains a major challenge: even the frontier models evaluated on ProgramBench fully resolve fewer than 1% of tasks. One obstacle is the lack of scalable training environments for this from-scratch setting, spanning the whole software engineering life cycle, as existing environment-construction frameworks focus only on a single phase in software development. To address this gap, we introduce MindForge, an automated pipeline that converts open-source command-line programs into source-free environments that expose only a compiled reference executable and its documentation. Using MindForge, we construct training environments from repositories disjoint from those in ProgramBench, and curate a high-quality data recipe consisting of program synthesis trajectories using GLM-5.2 as the teacher agent. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B on these trajectories increases its ProgramBench average test pass rate from 37.98% to 49.51%, achieving performance comparable to substantially larger frontier models. Moreover, the fine-tuned model consistently improves over the base model across all seven unseen software engineering benchmarks, spanning long-horizon repository generation and translation, bug fixing, feature implementation, and cross-language issue resolution, with absolute gains of 31.00 points on RepoZero-C2Rust, 14.16 on DeepSWE, 10.70/4.56 on NL2Repo-Bench (with/without tests), 5.04 on SWE-bench Verified, 5.93 on SWE-bench Pro, 5.22 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 4.94 on FeatBench.

## [Investigating reservoir computing for branch predictionin pipelined processors using emerging CMOS memristor devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27140v1)
*arXiv CS.LG* | 29/07/2026 | Score: 0.80
Tags: developer_tool, tool_update

> This project aimed to develop a novel reservoir compute (RC) implementation framework targeting high-speed operation and integration with CMOS digital logic. With the target workload of branch prediction (BP) for multistage pipelined central pro-cessing unit (CPU) cores. For this, a novel memristor based RC design framework was developed within the context of the workload requirements. This was then implemented in simulation using industry standard modelling languages of System Verilog (SV) and Verilog-AMS (VAMS).The developed RC design framework was subsequently verified using a basic sequence detection task before further benchmarking for its effectiveness at BP. The developed RC framework was tested using the Dhrystone performance benchmark, while targeting the RISC-V RV64GC instruction set architecture (ISA). Conducted testing demonstrates that RC shows great promise for ap-plication to BP and is capable of achieving impressive overall prediction accuracy. However, testing also shows that further refinement of the developed RC design framework is necessary to address shortfalls in the adaptability of the proposed RC system. As comparison against the state of the art TAGE predictor showed the proposed RC design framework to be 15x slower to adapt to changes in branching behaviour.
